title: Pointers
relevance: Pointers underpin C/C++ memory models, array/string handling, and systems interview questions about indirection, UB, and callbacks.

phases.goal: Establish that a pointer is a typed variable holding an address, distinct from the pointee, with &/* and NULL as core primitives.

must_hit.point: A pointer is a distinct variable whose value is a memory address bound to a pointee type (e.g. int * means an address where an int can be found), not merely a raw integer address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates container, location, and data; says the compiler uses the type to know how many bytes to read and how to interpret them.

must_hit.point: Address-of (&) yields a variable's memory address; dereference (*) follows a pointer to read or write the pointee.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through int x = 42; int *p = &x; and explains &x vs *p.

must_hit.point: NULL (typically 0 or (void*)0) is the sentinel for 'no valid object'; dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior and typically causes a segmentation fault.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions checking NULL before deref when origin is uncertain (e.g. allocation returns).

must_hit.point: Complex declarations are read with the Right-Left (spiral) rule: start at the name, look right, then left, expanding outward.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Parses int *p as 'pointer to int' and int *(*f)(int) as 'pointer to function taking int returning pointer to int'.

probes: What is a pointer, and how is int * different from treating an address as a plain integer?
How do you read a declaration like int *(*f)(int) using the right-left rule?

hints.1: Think house number on paper versus the family inside the house.
hints.2: Separate: variable value, variable address, and a pointer that stores that address plus pointee type.
hints.3: int *p = &x means p holds x's address; * tells the compiler p points to an int, so deref reads/writes an int-sized object.

phases.goal: Show how pointer arithmetic, const placement, void *, double pointers, and function pointers actually behave.

must_hit.point: Adding an integer to a pointer advances by n elements scaled by sizeof(pointee)—e.g. if int is 4 bytes and p is 0x1000, p + 1 is 0x1004—not raw +1 to the address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the tiled-floor / arr[4] example and states arithmetic is tied to pointee size.

must_hit.point: Pointer difference yields element count as ptrdiff_t; arithmetic and relational comparison are well-defined only for pointers into the same array (or one past the end).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists p+n / p-n, p2-p1, p1<p2 and flags unrelated-variable compare/subtract as UB.

must_hit.point: const int *p allows reseating p but not writing through *p; int *const p locks the address but allows *p writes; const int *const p locks both.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies right-left rule to each of the three forms and states what can/cannot change.

must_hit.point: void * is a typeless address: you cannot dereference or do pointer arithmetic on it; any object pointer converts to/from void * implicitly (e.g. malloc returns void *).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the compiler lacks size/scale, so typed assignment contextualizes the raw block.

must_hit.point: To let a function reassign a caller's pointer (e.g. char *), pass a pointer-to-pointer (char **); *buf = malloc(...) updates the original.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains allocate_buffer(char **buf) with &my_buf, or arrays of strings decaying to char **.

must_hit.point: A function pointer holds the address of executable code for callbacks; parentheses in int (*cmp)(int, int) are mandatory, else it parses as a function returning int *.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions typedef Comparator and passing ascending into sort_array / qsort-style use.

probes: If p points to an int at 0x1000, what is p + 1 and why?
Why does a function that reallocates a caller's char * need char **?

hints.1: Arithmetic steps by objects, not by single bytes, unless the pointee is a byte type.
hints.2: Scale factor is sizeof(pointee); const binds to what is immediately to its left under the right-left reading.
hints.3: p + 1 adds 1 * sizeof(int); for double pointers, pass &my_buf so *buf can overwrite my_buf itself.

phases.goal: Contrast when pointers are used for mutation versus for sharing without copy, and how arrays relate to but differ from pointers.

must_hit.point: Accepting a pointer does not imply mutation: e.g. size_t strlen(const char *str) uses a pointer to avoid copying a large string while const promises no write to the data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects 'passing a pointer guarantees modification' and cites const on the pointee.

must_hit.point: Arrays and pointers are distinct: an array is contiguous storage, but in most expressions the array name decays to a pointer to the first element; a[i] is identical to *(a + i).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States int a[5]; a yields &a[0] as int *, while noting they are fundamentally not the same thing.

must_hit.point: sizeof on an array name does not decay and yields the full array byte size (e.g. int arr[10] → 40 bytes), whereas sizeof on a pointer yields the pointer's size (typically 8 bytes on a 64-bit system).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts sizeof(arr) vs sizeof(p) when p = arr.

probes: Does passing a pointer always mean the callee will modify the caller's data?
How do sizeof(array) and sizeof(pointer) differ, and why doesn't the array decay under sizeof?

hints.1: Look at whether the parameter is pointer-to-const or pointer-to-mutable.
hints.2: Decay happens in most expressions, but sizeof applied directly to an array name is a special case.
hints.3: strlen(const char *) shares without copy and without mutation; sizeof(int arr[10]) is 40 bytes, sizeof(int *) is typically 8 on 64-bit.

phases.goal: Apply pointers safely in mutation, allocation via double pointers, callbacks, and classic operator/hazard pitfalls.

must_hit.point: *p++ dereferences the current address then advances the pointer (post-increment binds tighter but yields the old pointer); (*p)++ increments the pointee value; *(p++) is identical to *p++.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders the three expressions and states which object moves vs which value increments.

must_hit.point: Common hazards: uninitialized (wild) pointers hold garbage; dangling pointers refer to memory after free or after a local's lifetime ends; strict-aliasing violations (incompatible-type access) can silently corrupt under optimization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines dangling as pointee lifetime ended while the address value remains, and lists the three hazard classes.

must_hit.point: A function can swap two ints via int * parameters by reading/writing through *a and *b; to allocate into a caller's int *, use int ** and assign with *ptr = malloc(...).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes completing swap's *b = temp pattern and alloc_and_set writing **ptr = val after NULL check.

must_hit.point: Callbacks pass a function pointer (e.g. qsort comparator) whose signature must match; casting a mismatched function pointer risks severe undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions compare_desc(const void *, const void *) casting to const int * then returning descending order.

probes: What is the difference between *p++, (*p)++, and *(p++)?
What is a dangling pointer, and how does it differ from an uninitialized pointer?
How would you write a function that mallocs an int and makes the caller's pointer point to it?

hints.1: Check operator precedence and what post-increment returns.
hints.2: Wild = never initialized; dangling = was valid, lifetime ended; for allocation out-params, you need the address of the pointer.
hints.3: *p++ reads then p advances; (*p)++ changes *p only; void f(int **p){ *p = malloc(sizeof(int)); }.

tradeoffs.topic: Pointer parameter for mutation vs const pointer for shared read-only access
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A non-const pointer lets the callee write the caller's object; a const pointee pointer (as in strlen(const char *)) shares large data without copying while promising no mutation—so accepting a pointer alone does not mean modification.

An array is a contiguous object; a pointer is a separate address variable. In most expressions the array name decays to &a[0], and a[i] means *(a + i), but sizeof(array) does not decay and reports full array size, unlike sizeof(pointer).

Typed pointers support dereference and scaled arithmetic; void * is a raw address with no size/scale so you cannot deref or do arithmetic until you convert to a concrete type—useful for APIs like malloc that return untyped storage.

tradeoffs.topic: const int * vs int *const vs const int *const
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Pointer-to-const: reseatable, pointee immutable through that pointer. Const pointer: fixed address, mutable pointee. Const pointer to const: neither address nor pointee writable through that pointer.

gotchas.trap: Saying 'a pointer is a memory address'
gotchas.correction: A pointer holds an address and carries pointee type; the compiler uses that type for how many bytes to read (char * → 1 byte, double * → 8 bytes) and how to interpret them.

gotchas.trap: Assuming passing a pointer guarantees the callee will modify the caller's data
gotchas.correction: Pointers are also used to avoid copying; const on the pointee (e.g. strlen(const char *)) documents and enforces non-mutation.

gotchas.trap: Treating pointer arithmetic like integer +1 on the raw address, or comparing/subtracting pointers from unrelated objects
gotchas.correction: p + n advances by n * sizeof(pointee); difference is in elements (ptrdiff_t). Arithmetic/comparison are only well-defined within the same array (or one past the end); otherwise UB.
*p++ and *(p++) dereference the current pointer then advance it; (*p)++ increments the pointee value and leaves the pointer address unchanged.

gotchas.trap: Expecting sizeof(pointer) to equal sizeof(array) after p = arr
gotchas.correction: sizeof(arr) on int arr[10] yields the full array size (40 bytes) without decay; sizeof(p) yields the pointer size (typically 8 bytes on 64-bit).

gotchas.trap: Omitting parentheses in a function-pointer declaration: int *cmp(int, int)
gotchas.correction: Without parens around *cmp, it declares a function returning int *. Correct form is int (*cmp)(int, int); mismatched signatures cast to fit invite severe UB.

Wild pointers hold garbage until initialized; dangling pointers retain an address after free or after a local dies—both are invalid to touch. Always ensure a live object (and often NULL-check) before deref.
